name: Jade Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, I'm 27, and I work at Fernside, which is a cooperative farm owned by its workers and about 300 veg-box customers. We've got dairy goats, a few beef cows, about 60 acres of barley and beans, and three acres of market garden. I joined two years ago after doing bar work in the city, so I'm still very much the learner. I live with my girlfriend Priya, who works from home testing software, and between my savings and hers we're comfortable.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I help milk the goats, 70 of them, then I'm in the market garden weeding, planting out, or packing veg boxes on a Thursday. I use an AI planner on my phone every day to work out what needs sowing when, and I've started using it to draft the customer newsletter. I love the goats, they're like badly behaved dogs. What wears me out is weeding, honestly, hours on your knees between the carrot rows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, not magic, and that's fine. I'd post about how the planner saves me an hour a week on sowing dates. I'd also say the hype money should have gone into soil and farmworkers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my job stays the same, which is good, because I like it. Maybe a bit disappointing, because I was hoping for a weeding robot. My knees were hoping too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as normal, keep using the planner, and learn the cheese side properly from Marta. I'd put a bit more of my savings into the coop's member shares, because they're short of cash for a new goat shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a forecast for rain that never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. Would you be disappointed in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yeah. I'd hoped the tools would take the dull bits and leave the goats to me. But if it plateaus, I'm still better off than two years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to get better at on the farm, if nothing big changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheese. Marta makes a hard goat's cheese that sells out every week at the market, and she's 64. Someone needs to learn it before she retires, and I want it to be me.

S0.say: She'd say AI is useful, not magic, and that's fine. She'd also say the hype money should have gone into soil and farmworkers.
S0.think: Privately she thinks her job stays the same, which she's glad about. She's a little disappointed, because she was hoping for a weeding robot.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal and learns cheese-making from the farm's senior cheesemaker. Puts more savings into the cooperative's member shares to help fund a new goat shed.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, like rain that never comes.
S0.quote: Maybe a bit disappointing, because I was hoping for a weeding robot. My knees were hoping too.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is the rare farmworker who'd be let down by the plateau, because she wants the machines to take the dull work. She already uses AI daily for planning and writing. Her instinct is to put money into the cooperative rather than keep it for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why farms should be owned by the people who work them. If the robots are ours, the savings are ours too. I'd post that, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm probably in a good spot. I'm the one at Fernside who already uses the tools, so I'd likely end up setting them up. My bigger worry is wage farms where the boss keeps the savings and lets people go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a proposal for the members' meeting to trial a weeding robot in the market garden, and I'd use AI to compare models and costs. I'd go on any training going for it. And I'd join the regional land workers' alliance to push for rules on how robot savings are shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, if I'm honest. A little guilty for being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides at Fernside whether robots come in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The members, at the monthly meeting in the barn. It's one person one vote, so a weeding robot needs about 40 hands up. I'd have to bring cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the farm who'd lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who does most of the hand weeding with me. He likes it, weirdly, it's his quiet time. I'd want the coop to promise him the goat work or something else before the robot arrives.

S1.say: She'd say this is why farms should be owned by the people who work them. If the robots belong to the workers, so do the savings.
S1.think: Privately she thinks she's in a good spot as the person who already uses the tools. Her bigger worry is wage farms where the boss keeps the savings and lets people go.
S1.do: Writes a proposal to the members' meeting to trial a weeding robot and uses AI to compare costs. Joins a regional land workers' alliance to push for rules on sharing robot savings.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a little guilt about being excited.
S1.quote: It's one person one vote, so a weeding robot needs about 40 hands up. I'd have to bring cake.
S1.fieldNote: Her cooperative workplace shapes everything: she sees automation as something workers could own rather than suffer. The guilt about being excited is honest. She thinks of Pete, a colleague who likes the job she wants automated, which shows she sees the cost to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public ownership of this stuff, fast, because otherwise it all ends up with a handful of companies. I'd be out on marches and I'd be posting every day. Small farms and coops can't compete with that in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be worried, but not for my own bills. I'd worry that Fernside gets crushed by giant robot farms selling veg at half the price. My job's not the thing at risk, the whole idea of the coop is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the coop to buy whatever robots we could afford in the first six months, before prices jump. I'd put a big chunk of my savings into that, as member shares. And I'd join the national campaign for public AI, and help organise in our county.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really anxious. Not for me, for the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You were excited in the last picture. Does the speed change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, completely. Two years means no time for the members to vote slowly and bring cake. Either we move fast and borrow, or the big farms move faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your own savings in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it would go into Fernside, and Priya would kill me if I went over half. The rest stays as a cushion, because her job's at risk too, software testing is the first thing these things eat.

S2.say: She'd say we need public ownership of AI fast, or it all ends up with a handful of companies. She'd be marching and posting every day.
S2.think: Privately she's worried, but not about her own bills. She fears the cooperative gets crushed by giant robot farms selling veg at half the price.
S2.do: Pushes the cooperative to buy robots within six months, before prices rise, and puts a large part of her savings into member shares. Joins a national campaign for public AI and helps organise in her county.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly for the farm rather than herself.
S2.quote: Two years means no time for the members to vote slowly and bring cake.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version flips her excitement into worry, but the worry is about the cooperative model, not her income. Her plan is still to automate, just faster and with her own money. She notes her partner's job is exposed too, which tempers how much she'd risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but calmer: workers and communities need to own the machines. I'd want grants for coops and small farms to buy robots together. I'd say it at every farming meeting I could get into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for Fernside to be ready, if we start now. I'd honestly be all right. I'd be the one who runs the machines, and I'd learn the cheese too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do a short course in farm robotics, the kind the college runs online, and use AI tools to plan a five-year machinery budget for the coop. I'd move some savings into the coop now and keep some back. I'd get two neighbouring small farms to talk about sharing robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of hope mixed in. There's time to do this right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what's different from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between panic buying and planning. With two years we'd grab what we could. With five we could share a fleet of machines with the neighbours and not be in debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the machines at Fernside and two other farms, and making Marta's cheese. Priya says I'll be impossible. She's probably right.

S3.say: She'd say workers and communities need to own the machines. She'd want grants for coops and small farms to buy robots together.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is enough for the cooperative to be ready if they start now. She expects to be the one running the machines and making the cheese.
S3.do: Takes a short online course in farm robotics in the first year and uses AI tools to plan a five-year machinery budget. Moves some savings into the cooperative and gets two neighbouring farms talking about sharing robots.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with a lot of hope that there's time to do it right.
S3.quote: It's the difference between panic buying and planning.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her plan from a rush into a shared fleet with neighbours. She is confident about her own future and slightly embarrassed by it. Her politics show in wanting grants for groups rather than individuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build something fairer, if we bother. I'd want the government to fund local robot coops, like the old village machinery rings, where farms share kit. I'd post about it a lot, I'm told I'm annoying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine. I'll be 37, I'll know the farm properly by then, and I'll have spent ten years with these tools. If anything, I'm worried I'll get bored waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep putting money into the coop every year, do the robotics course when it makes sense, and push for the shared machinery idea with the neighbours. I'd start a little side project too, selling Marta's cheese online, with AI doing the orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time at your age. What does it change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can learn everything properly first, the goats, the cheese, the soil. Then when the machines come, I know what they should be doing. That's better than learning the robot before the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pete in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him there's ten years, and that I'll fight for him to have a place here. I'd also tell him to learn the goats, because they're too clever and too stubborn for any robot. He'd laugh, but he'd do it.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough to build something fairer. She'd want public funding for local robot cooperatives where farms share machines.
S4.think: Privately she thinks she's fine and will have ten years of experience and tools behind her by then. Her only worry is getting bored waiting.
S4.do: Keeps putting money into the cooperative each year and does the robotics course when it makes sense. Starts a side business selling cheese online with AI handling the orders.
S4.quote: That's better than learning the robot before the farm.
S4.fieldNote: Given ten years, she wants to master the farm first and the machines second, which is a thoughtful twist for an early adopter. She stays calm about her own position throughout the slower scenarios. Pete keeps coming back, which shows how much the cost to others weighs on her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because small farms like ours wouldn't have time to get ready and the big operators would eat us. What would help is cheap public loans for coops to buy machines together, and rules that stop a few companies owning all of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the goats. Everyone thinks robots will do farming, but goats climb on things, eat the cables, and escape through gaps you didn't know existed. I'd pay good money to watch a robot try to milk Duchess.

headlineQuote: I'd pay good money to watch a robot try to milk Duchess.
portrait: Jade Kowalski is a 27-year-old junior worker at Fernside, a cooperative farm with dairy goats, beef cows, cereals and a market garden. She lives with her girlfriend Priya, has solid savings, and uses AI every day to plan sowing and write the newsletter. She's progressive and wants workers and communities to own the machines, and in the slower scenarios she'd happily be the one running them. Only the two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, and even then her fear is for the cooperative, not for her own bills.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because small farms and cooperatives wouldn't have time to get ready and big operators would take over.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap public loans for cooperatives to buy machines together, and rules that stop a few companies owning everything.
